title: Supay, Lord of Uku Pacha
summary: The Aymara lord of the underworld Uku Pacha demands tribute from miners who dig too deep, and those who forget his offerings vanish into tunnels that have no end.
full_text:
Before the Spanish came, before the silver was torn from the mountains, the Aymara people knew that beneath the earth lived Supay — the lord of Uku Pacha, the underworld.

Supay was not evil. He was ancient, and ancient things do not conform to the narrow ideas of good and evil that humans invent to comfort themselves. Supay was the keeper of the seeds that had not yet sprouted, the guardian of the dead who had not yet been reborn, the ruler of the roots that held the mountains together.

When the miners came — first the Inca, then the Spanish, then the ones who came after — Supay watched from below. He did not hate them for digging. He hated them for their greed. There is a difference between taking what you need and taking everything you can reach.

The miners learned to respect Supay. They left offerings at the tunnel mouths: coca leaves, chicha, small figurines of silver. They whispered his name before entering the dark. They did not work on certain days, when the earth hummed with a sound that was not the sound of ore.

But some miners were too ambitious. They dug past the veins of silver into the veins of the earth itself. They broke through walls that were not meant to be broken. They found tunnels that curved in directions that had no names.

Those miners did not come back. Their names were forgotten. Their families said they had gone to the city, or to Argentina, or to anywhere but the mountain. But the other miners knew. They could hear whispers from the deep tunnels — not words, exactly, but the sound of someone mining in the dark, pulling silver from rock that had no silver, filling buckets with ore that had no value.

Supay's bargain was simple: take what you need, leave what you can, remember who was here first. The miners who kept this bargain grew old and rich. The miners who broke it grew thin and pale and were never seen on the surface again.

Today, in the mines of Potosí, the miners still leave offerings. They still whisper before entering the dark. The mountain still yields its silver — but only to those who ask politely.
moral: The earth gives generously to those who ask, but takes everything from those who merely take.
source: Aymara oral tradition, documented by Juan de Dios Yapita

title: Kusillo, the Hairy Trickster
summary: A small, hairy creature with reversed feet leads travelers in circles through the highland puna, mimicking their laughter to lure them deeper into the fog.
full_text:
In the highlands of Bolivia, where the puna stretches flat and featureless to every horizon, the Aymara tell of Kusillo — the hairy one.

Kusillo is small, no taller than a child. His entire body is covered in thick, dark hair, like the wool of a llama that has never been shorn. His face is hidden behind this hair, so that you see only his eyes — bright, curious, and not entirely trustworthy.

His feet are his most famous feature. They are backwards. Where a human foot points forward, Kusillo's foot points back. This means that when he walks toward you, his tracks lead away. And when he walks away from you, his tracks lead toward you.

Kusillo lives in the puna — the high, flat grasslands above the mountains, where the air is thin and the fog comes without warning. He is not malicious, but he is bored, and boredom in a trickster is a dangerous thing.

When a traveler crosses the puna alone, Kusillo appears. He walks alongside the traveler, just out of sight. He laughs — and his laughter sounds exactly like the traveler's own laughter, so that the traveler thinks: I must be going mad. Or: someone is following me. Or: perhaps I should turn back.

If the traveler turns back, Kusillo is satisfied. The traveler has been entertained, and Kusillo has been entertained, and no harm is done.

But if the traveler continues forward, Kusillo begins to lead. He walks ahead, leaving his backwards tracks, so that the traveler follows the tracks thinking they are fresh. But the tracks lead in circles. The puna is flat and featureless, and without the sun as a guide, there is no way to know which direction is which.

The traveler walks in circles. Kusillo watches from the fog, laughing his borrowed laughter. The fog thickens. The sun disappears. The traveler stops walking and waits for dawn.

In the morning, the traveler is found by herdsmen or by other travelers, sitting in the grass, confused but unharmed. Kusillo is gone. He has found someone else to amuse himself with.

The Aymara do not fear Kusillo. They respect him. They know that the puna is his home, and they are guests. They carry coca and leave small offerings when they cross the high grasslands. They do not travel alone when the fog is thick. And when they hear laughter that sounds like their own, they do not follow it.
moral: When the path ahead circles back on itself, stop walking and wait for the fog to lift.

title: The Muki in the Mine
summary: A dwarf-like spirit with enormous feet and a hat of silver lives in the deepest mines of Bolivia, guiding miners to rich veins — if they remember to share their coca.
full_text:
The miners of Bolivia have a friend. His name is Muki.

Muki is small — about the height of a man's knee — and his body is made of the earth itself. His skin is the color of raw silver, his hair is the color of copper ore, and his eyes glow with the dull red of cooling slag. He wears a hat shaped like an upside-down cone, the same shape as the funnels that carry ore to the surface.

His feet are enormous. They are flat and wide, like the paddles of a dredge, and they make no sound on the stone floor of the mine. When Muki walks through the tunnels, the miners hear nothing — only the drip of water and the creak of timber supports.

Muki lives in the deepest mines, where the tunnels narrow and the air thins and the timbers groan under the weight of the mountain. He does not come to the upper tunnels, where the air is good and the work is easy. He stays in the dark places, where the silver veins are richest and the danger is greatest.

Miners who respect Muki find silver. They leave offerings at the tunnel mouth — coca leaves, chicha, sometimes a small candle burning in the dark. When they enter the deep tunnels, they call out: "Muki, we are friends. We come to share the mountain." And Muki answers. Not with words — Muki does not speak. He answers with signs: a vein of silver exposed in the rock, a tunnel that leads to a chamber of ore, a pocket of gold where the geology says there should be only stone.

But miners who forget Muki — who take from the mountain without offering, who dig without asking, who work the deep tunnels in silence — those miners find nothing. Their picks strike barren rock. Their tunnels lead to dead ends. Their candles gutter and die in air that should be breathable.

And sometimes, in the deepest tunnels, miners who have forgotten Muki hear a sound behind them: the slap of enormous bare feet on stone. They turn and see nothing. But the sound follows them back to the surface, and it does not stop until they leave the mountain entirely.

Muki is not a spirit of the past. He is a spirit of the present. The miners of Potosí, Oruro, and Cerro Rico still leave offerings. They still call his name. And the mountain still yields its silver — to those who remember to share.
moral: The mountain shares its wealth with those who share in return.

title: The Abchanchu, Shapeshifter of the Road
summary: A shapeshifting vampire that appears as a beautiful stranger on the road, inviting travelers to share food and wine before revealing its true form — a skeletal figure that drinks the fat from human bodies.
full_text:
The Aymara of the Bolivian altiplano speak of the Abchanchu with the kind of fear that makes people cross themselves. It is not a ghost, not a demon, not a spirit. It is something older — something that was here before the gods were named.

The Abchanchu is a shapeshifter. It can appear as anyone: a beautiful woman, a lost child, an old man with a kind face. It stands by the side of the road — the lonely roads that cross the altiplano, where there are no houses for miles and the only company is the wind.

When a traveler approaches, the Abchanchu smiles. It asks for a ride. It offers food. It speaks kindly, asks about the traveler's family, tells stories about the road ahead. And the traveler, lonely and grateful for company, slows down.

That is when the Abchanchu strikes.

It does not attack with claws or teeth — not at first. It attacks with hunger. A hunger so deep and so old that it has become a kind of gravity. The traveler feels their body growing heavy, their thoughts growing slow, their strength draining away like water from a broken cup.

The Abchanchu feeds on fat. Not blood — fat. It drinks the fat from beneath the skin, from around the organs, from the marrow of the bones. A person fed upon by an Abchanchu becomes thin — not thin like someone who has not eaten, but thin like someone whose body has been hollowed out from the inside.

The Aymara say that you can recognize an Abchanchu's victim by the way they walk. They walk carefully, as if their bones might snap. They eat constantly but never gain weight. Their skin hangs loose and gray, like wet paper.

The only defense against the Abchanchu is to never stop for strangers on the altiplano. If someone appears on the road — no matter how beautiful, no matter how lost, no matter how much they need help — you must drive past. You must not slow down. You must not look back.

And if you must stop, carry coca. The Abchanchu cannot bear the smell of fresh coca leaves. It is the one thing that makes it flinch.

The roads of the altiplano are long and empty. The Abchanchu is patient. It has been waiting by the side of the road for centuries, and it will wait for centuries more.
moral: Not every stranger on a lonely road is what they appear to be.
source: Aymara oral tradition, documented by Waldo Álvarez

title: The Pishtaco of the Mountain
summary: A white-skinned stranger with a silver knife appears in mountain villages at night, draining the fat from sleeping farmers — because fat, in Aymara belief, is the substance of the soul.
full_text:
In the mountains of Bolivia, where the villages cling to the slopes like barnacles on a ship's hull, the people tell of the Pishtaco.

The Pishtaco is a stranger. He is always white — not white like snow, but white like the skin of someone who has never been in the sun. He is tall and thin and he wears clothes that do not fit the time or the place. He carries a silver knife.

He comes at night, when the village is asleep and the dogs are quiet. He enters homes without opening doors. He stands over sleeping farmers and cuts their skin — not deep, just enough to reach the fat beneath.

The Aymara believe that fat is not just fat. Fat is the substance of the soul. It is what makes a person strong, what makes a person alive. When the Pishtaco takes your fat, he takes your life force. You do not die — not immediately. You grow thin. You grow weak. You lose your will to work, to eat, to speak. You become a shell, and the shell walks and talks, but the person inside is gone.

The villagers know the Pishtaco is coming when the dogs howl at nothing. When the candles burn blue. When the shadows in the corners of the room seem deeper than they should be.

They defend themselves with fire. They keep candles burning all night. They place mirrors in the windows, because the Pishtaco cannot bear to see his own reflection. They hang bundles of herbs — rue, chamomile, coca — in the doorways.

But the Pishtaco is clever. He learns. He finds the houses with the dimmest candles. He enters through the roof, or the floor, or the spaces between the stones. He takes only a little from each person, so that the loss is not noticed until it is too late.

The only way to truly stop a Pishtaco is to catch him in the act. If you see him — if you can bring yourself to look at his face — he freezes. His silver knife drops from his hand. His white skin cracks and falls away, and beneath it there is nothing. Just the dark.

The Pishtaco has been walking through the mountains for centuries. He will walk through them for centuries more. The villages cling to the slopes. The farmers sleep. The dogs howl at nothing.
moral: The soul is not a spirit — it is the weight of your body, and it can be stolen as easily as fat from bone.
source: Andean oral tradition, documented by José María Arguedas

title: The Diablada of Oruro
summary: Every year during Carnival, the devils of the mine emerge to dance through the streets of Oruro, wearing masks of hammered silver and carrying pitchforks of twisted ore — a reminder that the mountain never forgets.
full_text:
Every year, in the month of February, the city of Oruro becomes a cathedral of devils.

The Diablada begins at dawn, when the first drum sounds in the Plaza 10 de Febrero. The dancers emerge from the side streets, wearing costumes that weigh as much as a man. The masks are enormous — hammered from tin and silver, studded with glass eyes that glow red in the sun. The pitchforks are real, made from twisted mine timbers.

The dance tells the story of the seven deadly sins. But it is not a dance about sin. It is a dance about the mountain.

The Aymara believe that beneath every mine, beneath every tunnel and shaft and chamber, there are devils. Not the devils of the Bible — those came later, with the Spanish. These are older devils. They are the spirits of the ore itself: the silver that resists being pulled from the rock, the tin that hides in veins too narrow for human hands, the gold that glitters in darkness no one has ever seen.

These devils do not hate humans. They respect humans. But they do not like being disturbed. They have lived in the mountain for millennia, in the dark, in the silence, in the cold. When humans come with their picks and their dynamite and their greed, the devils fight back — not with violence, but with fatigue. They make the timbers groan. They make the air thin. They make the candles flicker.

The Diablada is the miners' way of making peace. Once a year, they invite the devils out of the mountain. They give them masks to wear, costumes to dance in, music to move to. For one day, the devils are not prisoners of the dark. They are kings of the street.

The dance is slow and heavy. The devils move like men carrying the weight of the mountain on their shoulders. They stomp their feet, and the ground shakes. They raise their pitchforks, and the sun glints off the silver masks.

The people of Oruro watch from the sidewalks. They throw flowers. They light candles. They whisper names — the names of miners who did not come home, the names of tunnels that collapsed, the names of veins that ran out.

When the dance is over, the devils return to the mountain. The masks are put away. The pitchforks are hung on walls. The city goes back to being a city.

But the miners know that the devils are still there. They are always there. And next year, they will dance again.
moral: To make peace with the mountain, you must give its spirits a day in the sun.
source: Oruro Carnival oral tradition, documented by Ximena Medinacelli

title: the Acalica Water Spirits
summary: Tiny silver-skinned spirits that live in Lake Titicaca emerge at dawn to tend the reeds, and fishermen who see them must look away — or be drawn beneath the water to live among them forever.
full_text:
In Lake Titicaca, the highest lake in the world, the water is so cold that it burns and so deep that no one has found the bottom. The Aymara say this is because the lake has no bottom. It goes straight down, through the earth, to Uku Pacha — the underworld.

At the surface of the lake, where the reeds grow thick and the water is shallow, live the Acalica. They are tiny — no taller than a finger — and their skin is the color of polished silver. They have no hair. Their eyes are black and round, like drops of ink. They move through the water without making a sound.

The Acalica are the spirits of the lake's边缘 — the boundary between the water and the air, the living world and the dead. They tend the reeds as a gardener tends a garden. They weave the floating islands from totora reeds. They guide the fish through the underwater channels.

At dawn, when the sun touches the surface of the lake, the Acalica emerge. They sit on the floating islands and watch the sun rise. They do not speak — they communicate in a language of clicks and whispers that sounds like water over stones.

Fishermen who see the Acalica must look away. If you look directly at them, they look back. And when they look back, they see into you — into your memories, your fears, your desires. They see the part of you that belongs to the water, the part that has always wanted to sink beneath the surface and not come back.

If you look away, the Acalica are content. They return to their reeds. You return to your fishing. The lake gives you fish.

If you do not look away, the Acalica rise from the water. They are tiny, but their hands are strong. They take your wrists. They take your ankles. They pull you gently, gently, beneath the surface.

The water is cold. The water is deep. The water goes down, through the earth, to Uku Pacha. The Acalica guide you through the dark, through the tunnels, through the places where the dead wait to be reborn. They show you the roots of the mountains. They show you the seeds that have not yet sprouted.

You do not come back. Your boat is found drifting in the reeds. Your net is empty. The lake is still.

The Aymara do not fear the Acalica. They respect them. They leave offerings on the floating islands — coca, flowers, small boats made of totora. They fish only where the reeds are thin and the water is clear. And when the sun rises over Lake Titicaca, they look at the water, but not at what moves in it.
moral: Some beauty is not meant to be looked at directly.
source: Aymara oral tradition, Lake Titicaca region

title: the Amaru, Sacred Serpent of the Andes
summary: A massive winged serpent that lives in the deepest lakes of the Andes, carrying the bones of the dead between worlds — and when it surfaces, earthquakes split the mountains.
full_text:
The Amaru is not a snake. It is a serpent — which is to say, it is a snake that has grown so large and so old that it has become something else entirely.

The Amaru lives in the lakes of the Andes. Not the shallow lakes, not the lakes where the flamingos wade and the fishermen cast their nets. The deep lakes — the ones with no bottom, the ones where the water is black and cold and still.

In the deep lakes, the Amaru coils. Its body is as thick as a man's torso. Its scales are the color of wet obsidian. Its eyes are the color of copper ore. And on its back, between the scales, there are feathers — not bird feathers, but feathers made of light, the same light that flashes in the sky before an earthquake.

The Amaru is the carrier of the dead. When a person dies, their soul does not immediately go to Uku Pacha. It waits by the water's edge, in the reeds, in the mist. The Amaru comes for it. It takes the soul on its back and carries it down, through the water, through the earth, to the place where the dead wait to be reborn.

This is why earthquakes happen. When the Amaru surfaces — when it rises from the deep lakes to take a new soul — the water rises with it. The earth shakes. Mountains crack. Rivers change course. The Amaru does not intend to cause destruction. It is simply too large to move through the world without consequence.

The Aymara built their temples on the shores of deep lakes. They left offerings — gold, silver, coca, the bones of animals. They carved the Amaru's image into stone, so that it would know it was respected.

When the Spanish came, they mocked the Amaru. They called it a legend, a superstition, a fairy tale. They drained the shallow lakes. They dammed the rivers. They dynamited the mountains.

The Amaru did not forget. It still coils in the deep lakes. It still rises to carry the dead. The earthquakes continue. The mountains still crack. The rivers still change course.

The Aymara do not mock the Amaru. They do not forget it. They leave offerings by the water's edge. They carve its image into stone. They whisper its name when the earth shakes.

And the Amaru coils, and waits, and rises when it must.
moral: The earth remembers what it carries, and it shakes when it is disturbed.
source: Aymara/Quechua oral tradition, documented by María Rostworowski

title: the Phujku, the Harvest Demon
summary: A skeletal figure wrapped in dead corn husks stalks the fields at harvest time, draining the life from crops — and only the sound of bells and singing can drive it back to the earth.
full_text:
The Phujku comes at harvest time.

It is not a spirit of winter — winter is too clean, too honest. The Phujku is a spirit of the space between seasons, when the crops are dry but not yet gathered, when the fields are gold but not yet safe.

The Phujku is tall — taller than a man — and thin. Its body is wrapped in dead corn husks, dry and brittle, that rustle when it moves. Its face is a skull, but not a human skull. It is the skull of something that was never alive — something that grew without soil, without water, without sun.

It walks through the fields at night, when the farmers are asleep and the dogs are tied. It touches the corn, and the corn dies. It touches the potatoes, and the potatoes rot. It touches the quinoa, and the quinoa turns to dust.

The farmers know the Phujku is coming when the corn dries too quickly. When the husks crack and fall before they are gathered. When the fields smell of dust instead of grain.

They defend themselves with sound. They ring bells — not church bells, but small bells made of tin, the bells that hang from the necks of llamas and alpacas. They sing — not hymns, but the old songs, the ones that have no words, only rhythms that match the beating of a heart.

The Phujku cannot bear sound. Sound is life, and the Phujku is the absence of life. When the bells ring and the singing begins, the Phujku stops. Its husks stop rustling. Its skull turns toward the sound. And then it sinks into the earth, through the cracks between the furrows, down to the dark place where it lives.

But the Phujku is patient. It waits. It comes back the next year, and the year after that, and the year after that. It always comes at harvest time, when the crops are dry but not yet gathered, when the fields are gold but not yet safe.

The farmers ring their bells. They sing their songs. The Phujku sinks into the earth. The harvest is gathered. The granaries are filled.

And next year, the Phujku rises again.
moral: Life defends itself with noise. Silence belongs to the dead.
source: Aymara agricultural oral tradition, Cochabamba Valley

title: the Anata, Spirit of the Carnival
summary: An ancient spirit of joy and chaos that wakes each February to ride through the streets on the backs of devils, scattering flowers and coins and madness — because the Aymara believe that grief must be drowned in celebration.
full_text:
The Anata is the opposite of grief.

In the Aymara calendar, grief has its time. It comes in the long winter months, when the wind howls across the altiplano and the snow falls on the dead. It comes when the mines are quiet and the fields are frozen. It comes when the people sit in their houses and remember the ones who are gone.

But grief must not last forever. The Aymara believe that grief, left unchecked, becomes a poison. It seeps into the earth. It freezes the rivers. It silences the birds. It makes the world cold.

So in February, when the first rains come and the fields begin to green, the Anata wakes.

The Anata is not a single spirit. It is a force — the force of joy that rises from the earth when winter ends. It takes the form of a dancer, a fool, a clown. It wears a mask made of flowers and feathers. It carries a whip made of braided flowers. It rides on the back of a devil — not a real devil, but a dancer wearing a devil's mask, stomping through the streets with a pitchfork made of tin.

The Anata moves through the streets of the highland towns, scattering flowers and coins and chaos. It is not gentle. It grabs people by the arm and pulls them into the dance. It throws water on the quiet. It shouts at the silent. It laughs at the mournful.

The people who are pulled into the dance do not resist. They stomp their feet. They shake their hips. They shout and laugh and forget, for a moment, the weight of winter.

The Anata is not cruel. It is medicine. The Aymara believe that the body stores grief in the muscles, in the joints, in the bones. The only way to release it is to move — to dance until the grief is shaken loose, to shout until the grief is screamed out, to laugh until the grief is replaced by something lighter.

When the Anata passes, the streets are empty. The dancers are gone. The flowers lie on the ground, trampled and fragrant. The air smells of sweat and dust and joy.

The Anata sleeps again. It will wake next February, when the first rains come and the fields begin to green. It will ride through the streets on the back of a devil. It will scatter flowers and coins and chaos.

And the people will dance, because the alternative is to stop.
moral: Joy is not the absence of grief — it is the medicine that keeps grief from becoming a poison.
source: Aymara oral tradition, documented by Carlos Mamani Condori
